title: Bloom filter

definition.text: A space-efficient probabilistic data structure that tests whether an element is a member of a set, allowing false positives but never false negatives.

facts.text: A Bloom filter is a bit array of m bits, all 0 at first, plus k hash functions; adding an element sets to 1 the k array positions its hashes select.
To test an element, check its k positions: any 0 means it is definitely not in the set, while all 1s mean it is in the set or other elements set those bits by chance, a false positive.
False positives are possible but false negatives are not, and the false positive rate climbs as items are added, until every bit is 1 and every query answers positive.
A simple filter cannot remove an element, because clearing one of its bits could erase other elements and create false negatives; the counting variant replaces each bit with a counter.

With an optimal number of hash functions, a 1% false positive rate takes only about 9.6 bits per element whatever the element size, because the filter stores no items; the data itself needs separate storage.

Bigtable, HBase, Cassandra, ScyllaDB and PostgreSQL use Bloom filters to skip disk lookups for missing rows, LSM trees keep one per on-disk component, and a cache can check one so missing keys never hit the database.

Bloom's 1970 paper analyzes the trade-off between hash area size, the time to identify a message as a non-member (reject time) and an allowable error frequency, for testing messages one by one for set membership.

Its key claim is that allowing a few non-members to be falsely identified as members permits a much smaller hash area without increasing reject time, with a secondary, possibly slow test to catch those errors when necessary.

title: Counting Bloom filter
article: Bloom filter#Extensions and applications > Counting Bloom filters

definition.text: A Bloom filter variant whose array positions are counters instead of single bits, which lets it delete elements.

facts.text: A counting filter supports delete by widening each array position from one bit to a multibit counter; a regular Bloom filter is a counting filter with one-bit buckets.
Insert increments the counters its hashes select, lookup checks that each is non-zero, and delete decrements each one.
Counters are usually 3 or 4 bits, so a counting filter uses 3 to 4 times more space than a static Bloom filter, and counters must be large enough that overflow stays rare.
The table cannot be expanded, so the maximum number of keys must be known in advance, and the false positive rate grows rapidly once the designed capacity is exceeded.

definition.text: Set-membership filters such as cuckoo, quotient and xor filters that store short fingerprints of keys and can beat the classic Bloom filter on space, speed or deletion.

facts.text: Classic Bloom filters use 1.44log2(1/ε) bits per inserted key, but any structure in the same role strictly needs only log2(1/ε), so Bloom filters use 44% more space than an optimal one.

A cuckoo filter keeps short fingerprints of keys in a cuckoo hash table; a matching fingerprint means the key is probably in the set. It supports deletions and has better locality of reference than a Bloom filter.
Compared with the Bloom filter, a quotient filter has better locality of reference and supports deletions.

An xor filter stores fingerprints in a perfect hash table and is more memory efficient (1.23log2(1/ε) bits per key) and faster than Bloom or cuckoo filters, but it is harder to create and the set cannot be modified afterwards.

title: Cache filtering with a Bloom filter
article: Bloom filter#Extensions and applications > Cache filtering

definition.text: Using a Bloom filter to remember which URLs were requested so a web cache stores an object only when it is requested a second time.

facts.text: Nearly three-quarters of the URLs accessed from a typical web cache are one-hit-wonders, requested once and never again, so storing them wastes disk resources.
A Bloom filter keeps track of all URLs users access, and a web object is cached only when it has been accessed before, that is, on its second request.
Most one-hit-wonders are never written to disk, so the disk write workload drops, cache space is saved, and cache hit rates rise.
Akamai's servers use this to keep one-hit-wonders out of their disk caches, which significantly reduces disk workload and raises disk cache hit rates.

definition.text: A geocoding method that encodes latitude and longitude into a short alphanumeric string.

facts.text: A geohash is a hierarchical spatial index in a Base-32 alphabet: its first character identifies one of 32 cells, and that cell in turn contains 32 cells.
The world is recursively divided into smaller cells with each additional bit until the desired precision is reached, so a longer string means a more precise location and a smaller cell.
Points whose geohashes share a longer prefix are spatially closer; 9q8yy9mf and 9q8yy9vx are close because they share the prefix 9q8yy9.
Because a geohash is a plain string, a location is easy to store in a database column, and nearest neighbors can be found with simple string comparisons and efficient index searches.
Depending on its length, a geohash tells only that a user is somewhere within an area, which gives a degree of anonymity.

A geohash is a hierarchical spatial data structure that subdivides space into grid-shaped buckets, an application of the Z-order curve; removing characters from the end gradually reduces both the code size and the precision.
Data indexed by geohash keeps all points of a rectangular area in contiguous slices, which helps databases where queries on a single index are easier or faster than multiple-index queries.
The index also supports a quick-and-dirty proximity search, because the closest points are often among the closest geohashes.

definition.text: A tree data structure in which each internal node has exactly four children, used to partition two-dimensional space by recursively subdividing it into four quadrants.

facts.text: Each internal node of a quadtree has exactly four children, and the structure partitions a two-dimensional space by recursively subdividing it into four quadrants or regions; each child or leaf stores spatial information.
Quadtrees are the two-dimensional analog of octrees, which partition three-dimensional space.

Finding how close points are with latitude, longitude and Euclidean distance does not scale on large data sets because it is CPU-intensive, whereas a quadtree searches points within a two-dimensional range efficiently.
Subdividing a node only after a size threshold saves computation, and a mapping such as the Hilbert curve can improve range query performance further.
Quadtrees are used for spatial indexing and range queries, location-based services such as Google Maps and Uber, image processing and compression, mesh generation and sparse data storage.
A quadtree leaf cell represents a unit of interesting spatial information, and the subdivided regions may be square, rectangular or of arbitrary shape.

Quadtrees are also used for efficient two-dimensional collision detection, for solving multidimensional fields such as fluid dynamics and electromagnetism, and for image processing, where union and intersection of images are simple and fast.

definition.text: A way to find nearby businesses by building an in-memory quadtree of all locations and walking it down to the leaf that holds the search origin.

facts.text: The quadtree is an in-memory data structure, not a database; it runs on each location-based-service server and is built when the server starts.
The root node represents the whole world map and is recursively divided into 4 quadrants until no node has more than 100 businesses.

To find nearby businesses, traverse from the root to the leaf node containing the search origin; if it holds 100 businesses return it, otherwise add businesses from its neighbors until enough are returned.

Building a quadtree for 200 million businesses may take a few minutes, during which the server cannot serve traffic, so new releases roll out to a small subset of servers at a time to avoid a brownout.

definition.text: A distributed unique ID generator produces globally unique numerical IDs that are roughly sorted by time and generated at low latency by many machines.

facts.text: IDs used in social media should be roughly sorted by time, numerical values only, and highly scalable with low latency; each generator has its own pros and cons.
A UUID has 128 bits and is simple to generate without calling another service, but it is not sequential and is inefficient for database indexing, and ID conflicts, though unlikely, are possible.
A Snowflake ID is built from a timestamp, a machine ID and a serial number, with the first bit unused so IDs stay positive; it needs no network call to an ID service, so it is fast and scalable.
Snowflake implementations vary; for example, a data center ID can be added to the machine ID component to guarantee global uniqueness.
A database auto-increment column uses the database's transaction management to handle concurrent requests and guarantees uniqueness within one table.
Auto-increment IDs need network communication and may expose sensitive business data; as user IDs they give competitors a rough idea of the total number of registered users.
In the database segment approach, ID servers fetch IDs from the database in batches and cache them, each server handling a segment of IDs, which greatly saves I/O pressure on the database.
Redis can also generate unique IDs from a key-value pair, and because it stores data in memory this performs better than the database.

title: Limits of geohash proximity search
article: Geohash#Limitations when used for deciding proximity > Edge cases

definition.text: Using shared geohash prefixes to find nearby points works for most points but fails near cell borders, the poles and the 180 degree meridian.

facts.text: Geohashes that share a long prefix are close together, but the reverse is not guaranteed: two nearby points can have a short or no shared prefix.

Close points on opposite sides of the 180 degree meridian, near the poles, or either side of the Equator or Greenwich meridian get very different geohashes, because they lie in different halves of the world.

A bounding-box search between the southwest and northeast corner geohashes retrieves every point along the z-order curve between them, which can be far too many, and it breaks down at the 180 meridians and the poles.

Distance between two geohashes reflects distance in latitude/longitude coordinates, not actual distance; despite this, geohashing has been used for proximity search in Elasticsearch, MongoDB, HBase, Redis and Accumulo.

title: HyperLogLog

definition.text: An algorithm for the count-distinct problem that approximates the number of distinct elements in a multiset using very little memory.

facts.text: Counting distinct elements exactly needs memory proportional to their number, which is impractical for very large data sets; HyperLogLog makes a single pass over the data using an auxiliary memory of m units and returns an estimate.
Its relative accuracy, the standard error, is typically about 1.04/√m for m units of memory.
It estimates cardinalities well beyond 10^9 with a typical accuracy of 2% using only 1.5 kilobytes, and matches the accuracy of its predecessor LogLog with only 64% of LogLog's memory.
It hashes each element into a uniformly distributed random number and uses the maximum number of leading zeros in the binary forms of those numbers to estimate the cardinality.
A single estimate has a large variance, so the hashed values are split into many subsets, the maximum leading zeros is found in each, and a harmonic mean combines the estimates.

The state is an array of m registers set to 0; add hashes the element, uses its first b bits to pick a register, and keeps the larger of the register's value and the leftmost-1 position of the remaining bits.

Count combines the registers with a harmonic mean, and merge takes the maximum of each pair of registers to get the union of two sets; add is O(1), count and merge O(m), and the algorithm parallelizes optimally.

HyperLogLog is biased for small cardinalities, where Linear Counting is used; HyperLogLog++ adds a 64-bit hash, an empirical bias correction and a sparse register representation to cut memory for small cardinalities.

notes: Wikipedia sentences 3b2afba93ab5, 2a2ea27bca02 and f2dad12afbbe lost superscripts and the square root in extraction; the 1.04/√m standard error is stated from the paper abstract (954c43f2e0e8), whose TeX is intact.

definition.text: Quadtrees are classified by the kind of data they hold, such as areas, points, lines and curves, and by whether the tree's shape depends on the order data is added.

facts.text: A region quadtree decomposes a region into four equal quadrants and so on; each node has exactly four children or none, and tree height depends on the spatial distribution of interesting areas.

A point quadtree adapts a binary tree to two-dimensional points, with four pointers per node and every subdivision centered on a point; it usually runs in O(log n) time, though k-d trees have surpassed it.
A point-region (PR) quadtree stores a list of the points in each leaf cell instead of a uniform value, and, like the point quadtree, can grow to linear height on a bad set of points.
Edge quadtrees store lines and PM quadtrees store collections of polygons, while compressed quadtrees keep only subtrees with interesting data to avoid storing many empty nodes.

definition.text: A form of unique identifier used in distributed computing that packs a timestamp, a machine ID and a sequence number into one number.

facts.text: The Snowflake format was created by Twitter, which uses it for tweet IDs; the format has since been adopted by other companies such as Discord and Instagram.

A snowflake has 41 bits of timestamp in milliseconds since a chosen epoch, 10 bits of machine ID to prevent clashes, and 12 bits of per-machine sequence number, so several IDs can be made in one millisecond.
Only 63 bits vary, so the value is a non-negative number that fits in a 64-bit signed integer; the first bit is unused to keep IDs positive.
Snowflakes sort by creation time, and the creation time can be calculated from the ID, so objects created before or after a given date can be selected by ID.
A generator needs no network call to an ID service, so Snowflake IDs are fast and scalable.

Implementations vary: the original Twitter library splits the 10-bit machine ID into a 5-bit data center ID and a 5-bit worker ID, while Instagram uses 41 timestamp bits, 13 shard ID bits and 10 sequence bits.

title: Universally unique identifier

definition.text: A 128-bit number used to identify information in computer systems, generated without any central authority.

facts.text: A UUID is a 128-bit number, also called a GUID in software typically created by Microsoft; it is usually written as 32 hexadecimal digits in the 8-4-4-4-12 hyphenated format.

UUID uniqueness depends on no central registration authority or coordination between generators, so independent parties can label information that coexists in the same databases with negligible probability of duplication.
The probability that a UUID is duplicated is not zero but close enough to zero to be negligible; for properly generated version-4 UUIDs it is one in a billion within 103 trillion of them.
Collisions in time- and MAC-based UUIDs come only from deliberate construction or error such as skewed clocks or bugs, and random UUIDs need a high-entropy source of randomness.
The meaning of the bits is set by the variant, of which variant 1 is the most common; variants 1 and 2 have versions that further define the interpretation of the UUID.

UUIDs are commonly used as unique database keys, but the random nature of versions 3, 4 and 5 and the field ordering of versions 1 and 2 can hurt database locality and performance when they are primary keys.
Reordering time-based UUIDs so the timestamp comes first averts the insertion performance loss, which is the rationale for versions 6 and 7.
A UUID is 16 octets (128 bits); the variant field in the top bits of octet 8 determines the layout of every other bit, and the version number sits in the most significant 4 bits of octet 6.

notes: ByteByteGo's claim that a UUID does not guarantee global uniqueness is compatible with the Wikipedia statement that duplication is possible but negligible; stated as such, not as a conflict

definition.text: The UUID versions are the ways of filling a UUID's bits: time and node based, name hash based, random, time-ordered with random bits, or custom.

facts.text: Version 1 is time-based: a 60-bit timestamp counting 100-nanosecond intervals since 15 October 1582 UTC, a 48-bit node ID, usually a MAC address, and a clock sequence that avoids duplicates when the clock moves backwards.

Versions 3 and 5 are name-based: they hash a namespace identifier, itself a UUID, with a name, using MD5 for version 3 and SHA-1 for version 5, so systems derive the same UUID from a name without a registry.
Version 4 is made from random or pseudorandom numbers: six bits are fixed for variant and version, leaving 122 random bits, which gives 5.3×10^36 possible version-4, variant-1 UUIDs.

Version 6 is field-compatible with version 1 but stores the timestamp from most to least significant byte for better database locality; systems without legacy version-1 UUIDs should use version 7 instead.

Version 7 puts a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp in the most significant bits and fills the other 74 non-version, non-variant bits with random bits, optionally a sub-millisecond fraction or counter; implementations should use it instead of versions 1 and 6.

Version 7 UUIDs are monotonically ascending, creation-time-ordered, lexically sortable keys, so new records land at the end of the key sequence, unlike random version 4, whose keys scatter across it and hurt performance.

Version 8 is for experimental or vendor-specific use: only the version and variant bits are fixed, leaving 122 bits for custom content, and its uniqueness is implementation-specific and must not be assumed.
Versions 1, 2, 6 and 7 expose the time of generation, so UUIDs can reveal when a system went live, or its growth over time; the RFC calls the embedded timestamp a very small attack surface.

definition.text: A hash function maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, called hash values, hash codes, digests or hashes, which are usually used to index a hash table.

facts.text: A hash function and its hash table give access to data in small, nearly constant time per retrieval, with storage only fractionally greater than the data itself and far less than storing every possible key.
A hash function does three jobs: it folds variable-length keys into fixed-length values, scrambles the bits so values spread uniformly, and maps the values into the size of the table.
A good hash function is fast and spreads expected inputs evenly over its output range, because the cost of hashing methods rises sharply as collisions increase. Uniform is not the same as random.
A hash function must be deterministic: the same input must always give the same hash value, which rules out functions that depend on a pseudo-random number generator or the time of day.
Average-case behavior can be nearly optimal, but a poorly designed function, pathological keys or a high load factor can push access time toward linear in the number of items.

For a table size n that can change, compute a fixed wide-range hash and take the remainder after dividing by n. Resizing should move as few records as possible, which matters most in distributed hash tables.

Hash functions also build caches for large data sets on slow media, where a collision is resolved by discarding or writing back the older item, and they are an essential ingredient of the Bloom filter.
Hash tables may use non-cryptographic hash functions, while cryptographic ones secure sensitive data in integrity checking, message authentication codes, password storage and signatures.

definition.text: A hash collision happens when two distinct pieces of data share the same hash value.

facts.text: Hash functions are many-to-one, with far more possible inputs than output values, so collisions are inevitable by the pigeonhole principle: with more objects than hash values, a collision is guaranteed.

The birthday paradox makes collisions likely long before the output range is exhausted, and a birthday attack uses it: it is easier to find any two inputs that collide than one matching a specific value.

Cryptographic hash functions are designed so that finding a collision is computationally infeasible (collision resistance); non-cryptographic ones, used in Bloom filters, hash tables and count sketches, need only uniform distribution and the avalanche property.
Simple non-cryptographic hashes such as CRC have essentially no collision resistance, so they cannot be used on input an attacker can manipulate, for example against hash flooding attacks.
Hash tables handle collisions with a collision-resolution strategy; the two most common are open addressing and separate chaining.
In open addressing, cells are occupied, empty or deleted; on a collision the table is probed for an alternate empty cell, using linear probing, double hashing or quadratic probing.
In separate chaining, records that hash to the same cell go into a linked list in that cell. Keeping track of many lists can make the table slow.
The effect of collisions depends on the application: checksums minimize collisions between similar inputs, while hashes made to find similar data maximize them, using locality-sensitive hashing.

definition.text: String hashing folds the characters of a variable-length string into a fixed-size hash code.

facts.text: Strings have very uneven distributions, so a common fold multiplies a running total by a sizable prime constant, adds the next character and ignores overflow, then reduces the result with a modulo or mask to fit the table.

Information can cluster in the upper or lower bits of the bytes, for example because ASCII codes have a top bit of 0; the clustering survives into the hash and causes more collisions than a proper randomizing hash.
Hashing only the first and last characters or the middle of a string saves iterating over it, but such functions can readily become linear because of redundancies and clustering in the key set.
A rolling hash computes the hash of every k-character window of a text with effort proportional to mk + n rather than k·n, as in the Rabin-Karp substring search algorithm.

title: Similarity hashing
article: Hash function#Hashing variable-length data > Fuzzy hash

definition.text: Similarity hashing, or fuzzy hashing, produces hashes that show when data is similar but not identical.

facts.text: Fuzzy hashing detects data that is similar but not exactly the same, unlike cryptographic hash functions, which are designed to give very different hashes for even minor differences.
A perceptual hash fingerprints multimedia and is a type of locality-sensitive hash, so similar features give similar hashes; it is used to find online copyright infringement and in digital forensics.
Hashes meant to find similar data, such as homologous DNA sequences or similar audio files, are designed to maximize collisions between similar items, using locality-sensitive hashing.
Fuzzy hashing has been used to identify malware and could support data loss prevention and detecting multiple versions of code.

definition.text: MD5 is a widely used hash function that produces a 128-bit hash value, typically written as 32 hexadecimal digits.

facts.text: MD5 turns a message of any length into a 128-bit output by padding it and processing it in 512-bit blocks; a small change in the message gives a mostly different hash because of the avalanche effect.

MD5 is not collision-resistant, which was shown in 2004, so it is unsuitable for SSL certificates or digital signatures; collisions can be found within seconds, and the CMU Software Engineering Institute calls it cryptographically broken.

MD5 checksums still reveal a corrupt or incomplete download, but because collisions are easy to make they cannot protect against deliberate tampering, nor can a checksum fetched over the same channel as the file be trusted.
MD5 was historically used to store one-way password hashes, but NIST does not list it among the recommended hashes for password storage.

definition.text: A count-min sketch is a probabilistic data structure that serves as a frequency table of events in a stream of data.

facts.text: It uses hash functions to map events to frequencies but, unlike a hash table, takes only sub-linear space, at the expense of overcounting some events because of collisions.

The sketch is a two-dimensional array of w columns and d rows, with a separate pairwise-independent hash function for each row; w and d are fixed at creation and set the space, time and error probability.
To record an event of type i, each row j applies its hash function to get a column index and increments the cell at that row and column by one.
A point query returns the least value among the cells for i. It never underestimates the true count, and with probability 1 − δ it exceeds it by at most εN, where N is the total number of items seen.
Choosing w = ⌈e/ε⌉ and d = ⌈ln 1/δ⌉ keeps the error in answering a query within an additive factor of ε with probability 1 − δ.
The sketch is linear: summing the sketches of two streams gives the same result as sketching the concatenated streams, so it is mergeable and suitable for distributed as well as streaming settings.
The minimum estimator is biased, as it may overestimate but never underestimate; it works well on highly skewed distributions, and conservative updating, which changes only the update, reduces error.

A count-min sketch is used differently from a counting Bloom filter: it has a sublinear number of cells set by the desired approximation quality, while a counting Bloom filter is sized to the number of elements in the set.

definition.text: A Merkle tree, or hash tree, is a tree in which each leaf is labelled with the cryptographic hash of a data block and each inner node with the hash of its children's labels.

facts.text: A hash tree verifies a large data structure efficiently and securely: proving a leaf belongs to a binary hash tree takes hashes proportional to the logarithm of the leaf count, where a hash list needs the leaf count itself.
The root hash is obtained from a trusted source, while the tree itself can come from any untrusted peer; a tree that does not match the root hash is damaged or fake, and another source is tried.
One branch can be downloaded and checked at a time, even before the whole tree is available, so a file split into small blocks needs only the damaged blocks downloaded again.

Most hash trees are binary, though a node can have many more children; they usually use a cryptographic hash such as SHA-2, while non-cryptographic checksums such as CRCs suffice against unintentional damage only.

Hash trees help peer-to-peer networks check that blocks arrive unaltered, and are used in ZFS, Git, Bitcoin and Ethereum, Certificate Transparency, and NoSQL systems such as Apache Cassandra, Riak and Dynamo.
The root hash does not show the tree depth, which allows a second-preimage attack with a forged document; one fix prepends a 0x00 byte when hashing leaves and 0x01 when hashing internal nodes.

definition.text: A trie, also called a prefix tree or digital tree, is a search tree for storing and retrieving strings from a dictionary or set.

facts.text: Nodes do not store their keys: a node's position determines its key, edges stand for single characters, every child shares a common prefix with its parent, and the root represents the empty string.
Searching follows the key's characters from the root, and a null link means the key does not exist; the search takes O(m) time, where m is the length of the key.
Insertion follows the characters and creates new nodes wherever it meets a null link, storing the value in the last node. Deletion clears that value and removes nodes left with no children.

Compared with a hash table, a trie looks up a key in O(m) with no hash function and no collisions, and sorts keys lexicographically; it is less efficient on secondary storage with high random access time.

Each node has as many links as the alphabet has characters, 128 for ASCII, and most are null, so a pointer-vector trie is enormous; linked lists, bitmaps or alphabet reduction save memory at the cost of speed.
A radix tree, or compressed trie, merges any node that has only one child into its parent for better space and time; it works best when the trie is static and its keys are sparse.

Tries suit autocomplete and predictive text, spell checking and longest-prefix matching in IP routing, because lookups follow prefixes. Web search engines keep a compressed trie of searchable words, each leading to a list of URLs.

definition.text: The Z-order, or Morton, curve maps multidimensional data to one dimension while preserving locality: points close together in several dimensions usually lie close together in the order.

facts.text: The z-value of a point comes from interleaving the bits of its binary coordinates; two-dimensional z-values are also called quadkey values, and connecting them in numerical order draws a recursively Z-shaped curve.
Once the data are sorted by bit interleaving, any one-dimensional structure can hold them: arrays, binary search trees, B-trees, skip lists, or hash tables with the low bits truncated.

The order equals a depth-first traversal of a quadtree or octree, so sorting points by z-order builds a compressed quadtree efficiently, since the points in any quadtree square form a contiguous interval.

A multidimensional range query cannot simply use binary search. From the z-value reached, the search computes the next z-value inside the range (BIGMIN, or LITMAX when searching downward) and skips the stretch between.

The method does not depend on the one-dimensional structure, so balanced trees handle dynamic data with O(log n) insertion and deletion, and it fits existing databases more easily than R-trees, which need special handling.
Z-order is one of the few multidimensional access methods that has found its way into commercial database systems.
The Hilbert curve has been suggested as an alternative with better order-preserving behaviour and is used in the S2 geometry index; Geohash is based on the Z-order curve.
Some GPUs store texture maps in Z-order so that cache lines represent rectangular tiles, raising the chance that nearby accesses hit the cache.

definition.text: The Hilbert curve is a continuous space-filling fractal curve, first described by David Hilbert in 1891, that maps between one and two dimensions while preserving locality fairly well.

facts.text: Mapping between 1D and 2D along the Hilbert curve keeps points that are close in one dimension close after folding, and this locality property is why the curve is widely used in computer science.
The locality property has been used to index geospatial location data; Singh's Uber design applies mapping algorithms such as the Hilbert curve to run range queries that find nearby drivers.
For multidimensional databases the Hilbert order has been proposed instead of Z order because it preserves locality better; Hilbert curves have been used to compress and accelerate R-tree indexes.

The distance of a point along the curve can be converted to coordinates in n dimensions and back by standard techniques such as Skilling's method, and the curve works even when the data space is not a square.

title: K-d tree

definition.text: A k-d tree is a space-partitioning data structure, a binary tree whose nodes are points, for organizing points in a k-dimensional space.

facts.text: Each non-leaf node implicitly defines a splitting hyperplane perpendicular to one of the k axes: points on one side of it go to the left subtree and points on the other side to the right subtree.
In the canonical construction the splitting axis cycles as you go down the tree and each node takes the median point on that axis, which yields a balanced tree with leaves at about the same depth.
Inserting a point and removing one each take O(log n) in a balanced tree. Repeated insertion can unbalance the tree, and rotations cannot rebalance it because it is sorted in several dimensions.
Nearest-neighbor search descends as if inserting the query point, saves the point at the leaf as the current best, then unwinds the recursion, updating the best at each node.

At each node it checks whether a hypersphere around the query, with the current best distance as radius, crosses the splitting plane. If it does, the other branch is searched; if not, that whole branch is eliminated.
The search can return the k nearest neighbors by keeping k current bests, or become approximate by capping the number of points examined, which helps in real-time uses such as robotics.
Range searches, such as members aged 20 to 50 with incomes from 50,000 to 80,000, suit k-d trees because each level divides the range of a domain in half.

In low dimensions the nearest point is found in O(log n) on average, but the curse of dimensionality makes high-dimensional search evaluate most points, no better than exhaustive search, so approximate nearest-neighbour methods are advised.

notes: Sentence b3fca07139d3 (n much greater than 2^k) lost its superscript in extraction, so the rule of thumb for how many points a k-dimensional tree needs is not stated as a fact.

definition.text: Base64 is a binary-to-text encoding that represents each 6-bit segment of the data with one of 64 printable characters, so binary data can travel over channels that carry only text.

facts.text: Each 6-bit group maps to one character of the alphabet, so Base64 produces four characters for every three input bytes; the encoded data is 33% larger, plus about 3% more if line breaks are inserted.
When the input is not a multiple of three bytes, the last group is padded with = characters: one = after two leftover bytes and two after one, and the decoder discards the padded zero bits.
Padding is not essential for decoding, because the length of the encoded text reveals the number of missing bytes, but when Base64 strings are concatenated, padding is required to avoid ambiguity.

The alphabet typically uses A-Z, a-z and 0-9 for the first 62 values and, in many variants, + and / for the last two; RFC 4648 describes the most common alphabet, and most variants differ only in the last two.

RFC 4648 also defines a URL and filename safe alphabet for compact identifying information, such as a 128-bit UUID in an HTTP parameter; Base64url, as used in JWTs, differs by its non-alphanumeric characters and omits padding.

Base64 embeds binary data such as images in HTML, CSS and XML, and carries e-mail attachments, because SMTP was originally designed to transport only 7-bit ASCII; MIME sets a maximum line length of 76 characters.
Some systems use other alphabets or orderings; bcrypt and Unix crypt put . and / before the alphanumeric characters, so their encoding is not compatible with RFC 4648 Base64.

definition.text: RFC 9562 advises how to generate, store, sort and protect UUIDs so that they stay unique, sortable and safe to use in databases and distributed systems.

facts.text: Where feasible, store UUIDs in a database as the 128-bit binary value: text needs 288 bits for the same value, while binary takes less space and may be faster, and text is simpler when the text form is needed.
Time-ordered monotonic UUIDs sort as opaque raw bytes and give database-index locality because new values sit near each other; the gap from random inserts can be one order of magnitude or more.

Schema designers are cautioned against name-based UUIDs as primary keys, because the name input, such as a postal code or license number, can later change; time-based surrogate keys are the general advice.

Time-based UUIDs are normally monotonic through the embedded timestamp, but batches created within one tick need a counter: dedicated counter bits after the timestamp, a randomly seeded counter, or extra clock precision in up to 12 bits.

As more nodes generate UUIDs independently, collisions become likelier. An embedded pseudorandom node ID, using version 8, adds collision resistance; a central registry that checks uniqueness can become a bottleneck and is not recommended.

Random bits should come from a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator, which gives both unguessable and unique values, and its state must be reseeded after changes such as process forks.

Implementations must not assume UUIDs are hard to guess or use them as security capabilities, identifiers whose mere possession grants access; if UUIDs are needed in a security operation, version 4 should be used.

Weigh the consequences of a collision: a duplicate log entry is low impact, but where failure is unacceptable an application must use as much collision resistance as its context allows. Treat UUIDs as opaque and avoid parsing them.
